claims.claim: Salesforce is positioning its CRM/data estate as an enterprise coordination layer for agentic software: customer data and workflow context feed Agentforce, while acquisitions extend data and agent capabilities. The human need served is lower-friction sales/service/operations work, but value depends on reliable data integration and measurable workflow outcomes rather than agent deployment counts alone.

Substitutes include hyperscaler AI stacks, point automation vendors and internally built agents; Salesforce is more resilient where embedded CRM data, permissions and workflow integration create switching costs, but less resilient where model capability commoditizes and customers can orchestrate agents outside Salesforce.

causalEdges: enterprise customer data + workflow context -> agent relevance -> automation adoption
embedded CRM permissions/workflows -> switching friction -> platform resilience
AI model commoditization -> easier external orchestration -> pressure on platform differentiation

risks.risk: Agent value may accrue to model/orchestration layers outside Salesforce if CRM context becomes portable.

unknowns.unknown: Incremental retention, margin and productivity attributable specifically to Agentforce are not isolated in current evidence.

claims.claim: Headline growth and AI momentum require decomposition: FY27 guidance includes acquisition contribution and management separately identified only part of the raise as organic, while AI ARR definitions and acquisition effects can make narrative growth outpace directly comparable organic economics.

risks.risk: Acquisition-heavy expansion can obscure organic growth quality and adds integration/capital-allocation risk.
AI ARR growth is not equivalent to proven incremental margin or retention.

contradictions.contradiction: Headline 11%-12% FY27 growth guidance includes acquisition contribution while management separately described only $100M of the guidance raise as organic growth.

unknowns.unknown: Organic Agentforce economics after excluding acquisitions remain insufficiently isolated for underwriting.
